newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt faces "total war" from media backers.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt faces "total war" from media backers.

text.p: The Russian government faced a growing crisis on Tuesday as media run by powerful businessmen who backed Boris Yeltsin's re-election campaign turned on top ministers, accusing them of corruption in the sale of state assets.

Boris Nemtsov, the young reformer and possible presidential contender, was singled out for attack after Friday's sale of a quarter of the state telephone company. He hit back at his critics, accusing them of "bandit capitalism" and "blackmail by media".

"Total information war" was business daily Kommersant's view of the mud-slinging after a consortium led by banker and former cabinet minister Vladimir Potanin, 36, and including U.S. financier George Soros, won the share tender for Svyazinvest.

Kremlin sources said containing the feud was a priority for the government and for Nemtsov's fellow First Deputy Premier Anatoly Chubais, the powerful economic reform chief who ran Yeltsin's campaign.
The row has destroyed any semblance of solidarity among the group of businessmen who quietly rallied their media muscle and money behind Yeltsin to prevent a communist victory last July.
Insiders say their reward was state assets at knock-down prices. But relations among them have worsened, with several disputes over murky state auctions ending up in the courts.
Most worrying now for ministers, one political source said, was that so many big banking and media interests were lining up against the government and Potanin, the head of Uneximbank.

Nemtsov, in an interview published on Tuesday by a newspaper in which Potanin has a stake, said the government was determined it would no longer share out "free assets" among the "group of seven bankers". Some of them might therefore try to force him from office, he said, or cut a deal with the opposition.

"They are going to fight us with all they have. Right up to us having to quit," Nemtsov told Komsomolskaya Pravda. "The interests of some finance-media groups could merge with the interests of the communists and fascists."
Nemtsov, a telegenic 37-year-old liberal, was summoned by Yeltsin to clean up government and the economy in March.

"When I started work, the president and I agreed...there would be no more bandit capitalism," Nemtsov told reporters in the central city of Cheboksary on Tuesday. "We will take a civilised path and will hold honest sales of state assets."

Nemtsov said Potanin's group won the Svyazinvest auction fairly with the highest bid. It would allow the government to pay its wage debts to doctors and soldiers. But the losers, he alleged, had wanted an old-style backroom carve-up on the cheap.
Senior political sources said the losing consortium was led by Russian tycoons Vladimir Gusinsky, who controls NTV television and Sevodnya newspaper, and Boris Berezovsky.

Berezovsky said he suspended his business interests when Yeltsin named him to the Kremlin Security Council last December. His empire includes Nezavisimaya Gazeta daily and a large stake in ORT television, in which the state also owns 51 percent.
Berezovsky has not commented on the Svyazinvest deal. Gusinsky's Most group hotly rejected Nemtsov's allegations.
NTV, ORT, Nezavisimaya and Sevodnya carried bitter attacks on Potanin, Nemtsov and privatisation minister Alfred Kokh.

NTV, which has generally supported the liberal reforms, said unnamed bankers were using privatisations to raise funds for a presidential campaign by Nemtsov in the year 2000: "Everyone needs money but above all those who thirst for power need it."
ORT television presenter Sergei Dorenko told Kommersant on Tuesday that Nemtsov was "twitching" like a "cockroach".
A senior government source said Chubais personally turned down pleas from Berezovsky and Gusinsky that they be awarded Svyazinvest. "Chubais told them those days are over," he said.
The media have yet to attack Chubais, however. He is seen as a kingmaker at the next election, but not a candidate himself.
The economic outcome of the latest row is far from clear.

Several other big sales are coming up, including the Rosneft oil company and 38 percent of Norilsk Nickel, one of the world's biggest metals producers. Uneximbank will auction it for the government. Norilsk stock slumped 17 percent on Tuesday when it announced plans to double its capital by issuing new shares.
At a political level, one Kremlin source even forecast that Nemtsov might be deliberately put in a tight spot by his Kremlin allies to test his mettle as a possible presidential candidate.
